t: The testis, spermatogenesis and male reproductive hormones
sub: How Sertoli and Leydig cells split the work, how sperm are built and delivered, and how LH, FSH and testosterone control it all.

pretest.q: Which testicular cell responds to FSH and secretes inhibin B?
pretest.why: Sertoli cells carry the FSH receptor. FSH drives them to make androgen-binding protein and inhibin B, and inhibin B then travels to the pituitary to suppress FSH selectively.

w.Leydig cell: Leydig cells sit in the interstitium outside the tubules and respond to LH by making testosterone; they make no inhibin.
w.Spermatogonium: Spermatogonia are germ stem cells resting on the basement membrane that divide by mitosis; they depend on Sertoli support and secrete no hormones.
w.Peritubular myoid cell: Myoid cells are contractile cells wrapped around the tubule that squeeze sperm toward the rete testis; they have no hormone-secreting role.

pretest.q: Where do sperm first gain the ability to swim forward?
pretest.why: Sperm are released into the tubule lumen fully formed but immotile. They acquire forward motility while passing through the head and body of the epididymis and are stored in its tail until ejaculation.

w.Seminiferous tubule: Spermiation releases finished but immotile sperm into the lumen, and fluid flow carries them passively out of the testis toward the rete testis.
w.Seminal vesicle: Sperm do not enter the seminal vesicles; these glands add fructose-rich alkaline fluid at the ejaculatory duct during emission.
w.Female reproductive tract: The female tract adds capacitation, hyperactivated motility and the acrosome reaction, but sperm already swim forward when they are ejaculated.

pretest.q: Which enzyme converts testosterone into the androgen that drives prostate growth?
pretest.why: Type 2 5-alpha-reductase in the prostate and genital skin converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a more potent androgen; finasteride blocks it and shrinks the prostate.

w.Aromatase: Aromatase, mostly in fat, converts testosterone to estradiol, which closes growth plates and feeds back on LH rather than enlarging the prostate.
w.17-alpha-hydroxylase: This enzyme works early in steroid synthesis, steering pregnenolone toward cortisol and androgen precursors; it does not act on testosterone.
w.Desmolase: Desmolase, the side-chain cleavage enzyme, turns cholesterol into pregnenolone as the first committed step of every steroid, long before testosterone exists.

body: How is the testis built, and which cell answers which hormone?

The testis is wrapped in a tough capsule, the **tunica albuginea**, whose septa divide it into lobules packed with coiled **seminiferous tubules**, which make up about 90 percent of its volume; small testes therefore usually mean poor sperm production. Tall Sertoli cells reach from the basement membrane to the lumen, and germ cells mature between them, from spermatogonia at the edge to spermatozoa at the center. Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the {{rp19btb|blood-testis barrier}}, which hides meiotic germ cells, whose antigens first appear at puberty, from the immune system. Outside the tubules, in the interstitium beside the capillaries, sit the **Leydig cells**, which make testosterone.
Sertoli answers FSH; Leydig answers LH

**Sertoli cells** carry the FSH receptor and make {{rp19abp|androgen-binding protein}}, which holds testosterone inside the tubule, plus inhibin B and, in the fetus, anti-Müllerian hormone. **Leydig cells** carry the LH receptor and make testosterone; they are rich in smooth endoplasmic reticulum and may contain {{rp20reinke|Reinke crystals}}. Sertoli cell number is fixed after puberty, so it caps sperm output.

Spermatogenesis fails at core body temperature and works best 2 to 4 degrees Celsius cooler, which is why the testis hangs in the scrotum. The tunica vaginalis, a sac of peritoneum carried down during descent, covers its front and sides, and the testis hangs from the **spermatic cord**, which carries the ductus deferens, testicular artery, nerves, lymphatics and the {{rp19pamp|pampiniform plexus}}. These veins wrap the artery and cool incoming blood by countercurrent exchange. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein and the right into the inferior vena cava, and testicular lymph runs to **para-aortic** nodes, not inguinal ones, because the testis began on the posterior abdominal wall.
How does a spermatogonium become a sperm, and how long does it take?

**Spermatogenesis** runs from the basement membrane toward the lumen. Diploid spermatogonia divide by mitosis, keeping a reserve and sending committed daughters inward. Primary spermatocytes then enter meiosis I, whose long prophase makes them the largest, most visible germ cells on a biopsy. Secondary spermatocytes finish meiosis II within hours, so they are rarely seen, and yield haploid spermatids. The last stage, {{rp19spermio|spermiogenesis}}, involves no division: the Golgi apparatus builds the **acrosome**, a centriole grows the flagellum, mitochondria wrap the midpiece and Sertoli cells engulf the shed cytoplasm. The sequence takes about 64 to 74 days, and epididymal transit adds about 2 weeks.
From stem cell to spermatozoon, in order
Diploid stem cells on the basement membrane renew themselves and send committed daughters inward past the Sertoli tight junctions.
These cells have already copied their DNA, and their long prophase is why they dominate a testicular biopsy.
The second division takes only hours, so these cells are seldom seen, and each yields two haploid spermatids.
Without dividing, each spermatid builds an acrosome, condenses its nucleus, grows a tail and sheds its extra cytoplasm.
Sperm are released and then matured
Spermiation frees immotile sperm into the lumen; they gain motility in the epididymis and fertilizing ability only in the female tract.
Today's semen analysis reports on events 3 months ago

Because spermatogenesis plus epididymal transit takes about **3 months**, a fever or new drug 6 to 10 weeks ago shows up in today's sample, and a treatment needs at least 3 months before a repeat **semen analysis** can judge it. Motility is gained in the epididymis, while capacitation and the acrosome reaction happen in the female tract, never in the testis.
Which ducts and glands do sperm pass, and what does each add?

Sperm leave the tubules through the **rete testis**, a network of channels in the mediastinum of the testis, and pass through the efferent ductules, which reabsorb most of the testicular fluid. The ductules join the single coiled duct of the **epididymis**, whose pseudostratified columnar lining carries **stereocilia**: long, nonmotile microvilli that absorb fluid while sperm mature from head to body and are stored in the tail. From the tail, the ductus deferens (vas deferens), with its thick smooth muscle wall, runs up in the spermatic cord, joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct and opens into the prostatic urethra. Sperm themselves make up only about 5 percent of semen volume.
If it is blocked or missing
Azoospermia with normal testis size and FSH
No sperm, but normal volume and fructose
Highly folded mucosa, no corpora amylacea
About 65 to 75 percent of volume: alkaline, **fructose**-rich fluid
Glands with papillary infoldings, corpora amylacea
About 20 to 30 percent: PSA, citrate, zinc

Knowing what each gland adds predicts what a blockage does. A **vasectomy** cuts only the path for sperm, so the ejaculate keeps its normal volume, alkaline pH and fructose but contains no sperm, and the breach of the barrier often leads to antisperm antibodies. Congenital absence of both vasa, usually from CFTR mutations, or an **obstructed** ejaculatory duct also removes the seminal vesicle fluid, so the sample is scant, acidic and fructose-negative with **azoospermia**. In both cases the testis keeps making sperm, so testis size and FSH stay normal; small soft testes with a high FSH instead mean failed sperm production.

body.q: After a vasectomy, a man's semen volume barely changes, but no sperm appear. Which reasoning best explains this?
o: The testis stops making sperm once the vas is cut, and sperm made up most of the semen volume
The prostate enlarges after the operation and replaces the lost volume with extra prostatic fluid
The epididymis takes over from the seminal vesicles and secretes the fructose that keeps the volume normal
Sperm make up only about 5 percent of semen, and the seminal vesicles and prostate, which empty beyond the cut, still add their fluid
body.why: The ductus deferens carries only sperm, about 5 percent of the ejaculate. The seminal vesicles, which supply most of the volume and the fructose, and the prostate, which adds PSA and citrate, empty into the ejaculatory duct and urethra beyond the cut, so their fluid still arrives. The testis keeps making sperm, which are broken down in the epididymis. A scant, acidic, fructose-negative sample would instead mean that seminal vesicle fluid is missing, as with absent vasa or a blocked ejaculatory duct.

body: The prostate shows tubuloalveolar glands with papillary infoldings, a two-cell lining of secretory and basal cells and, in older men, round laminated concretions called **corpora amylacea**; the seminal vesicle has a folded lining but no corpora amylacea, which is how the two are told apart. The prostate's zones predict its diseases. The **peripheral zone**, posterior and felt on rectal exam, gives rise to most cancers, while the **transition zone** around the urethra is where benign prostatic hyperplasia arises; the central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely diseased.
How do LH, FSH and feedback control the testis?

The hypothalamus releases GnRH in pulses, and the pulses matter: continuous GnRH, as from a long-acting agonist, desensitizes the pituitary and shuts the axis down. Each pulse releases LH, which drives Leydig cells to make **testosterone**, and FSH, which drives Sertoli cells to make androgen-binding protein and **inhibin B**. Testosterone and the estradiol made from it exert **negative feedback** on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH and LH, while inhibin B suppresses FSH alone. So when germ cells are lost and inhibin B falls, FSH rises while LH and testosterone stay normal. Androgen-binding protein keeps testosterone inside the tubule at 50 to 100 times the serum level.

Testosterone reaches its targets in three forms. Acting itself, it builds the fetal Wolffian ducts and, after puberty, supports spermatogenesis, muscle, red cell production and libido. In the prostate, genital skin and hair follicles, **5-alpha-reductase** converts it to **dihydrotestosterone** (DHT), a more potent androgen that shapes the fetal external genitalia and later drives prostate growth, male-pattern baldness and sebaceous activity. Through aromatization in fat, testosterone becomes estradiol, which closes the epiphyses, maintains bone and feeds back on the axis; obesity therefore gives low testosterone, high estradiol and low LH. With **aging**, total testosterone falls about 1 percent a year after 40, and rising SHBG makes free testosterone fall faster.
Low libido, lost muscle and bone, anemia
Tall stature and osteoporosis in aromatase deficiency
High FSH with normal LH after germ cell loss
Why does a man who injects testosterone become infertile even though his blood testosterone is high?

Spermatogenesis depends on testosterone inside the tubule, not in the blood. Normally LH drives Leydig cells to make testosterone locally, and androgen-binding protein keeps its concentration many times higher than in serum. Injected testosterone raises the serum level, which triggers negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so LH and FSH fall. Without LH the Leydig cells go quiet, intratesticular testosterone collapses and sperm production stops, leaving azoospermia and small testes despite a high serum value. Recovery takes months, because a new wave of sperm needs about 3 months to reach the ejaculate; hCG, which acts like LH, or clomiphene can preserve fertility instead.
How do nerves, vessels and nitric oxide produce an erection?

The penis contains three columns of **erectile tissue**: two dorsal corpora cavernosa and a ventral corpus spongiosum, which surrounds the urethra and forms the glans. Each is a sponge of endothelium-lined vascular sinusoids with smooth muscle trabeculae, and the corpora cavernosa are wrapped in a dense, inelastic tunica albuginea. Sexual stimulation activates parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4), which release **nitric oxide**. Nitric oxide raises **cGMP**, which lowers calcium and relaxes the smooth muscle, so the helicine arteries dilate and the sinusoids fill. The swollen sinusoids press the small veins against the tunica albuginea, the {{rp19venoocc|veno-occlusive mechanism}}, trapping blood so the penis becomes rigid.

Erection ends when phosphodiesterase type 5 (**PDE5**) breaks cGMP down and sympathetic tone returns. PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil preserve the cGMP that nitric oxide generates rather than starting an erection, so they need sexual stimulation, and they are dangerous with nitrates, which also raise cGMP and can cause severe hypotension. **Emission** is sympathetic: hypogastric nerves from T10 to L2 contract the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate while alpha-1 receptors close the bladder neck. **Ejaculation** itself is somatic: the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) drives rhythmic bulbospongiosus contractions, which is why alpha-1 blockers can cause retrograde ejaculation with a normal orgasm.

grid.q: Which of these are functions of Sertoli cells?
items: Form the blood-testis barrier with tight junctions
Secrete anti-Müllerian hormone in the fetus
Engulf residual cytoplasm shed by spermatids
Support developing germ cells as nurse cells
Secrete testosterone in response to LH
Contract to push sperm toward the rete testis
Secrete fructose into the seminal fluid
